lead: A mass transfer coefficient depends on velocity, length, density, viscosity and diffusivity. Measuring it for every fluid and speed is hopeless. So we pack those variables into three dimensionless numbers — Sherwood, Reynolds and Schmidt — and fit one curve through many experiments. Feed in Re and Sc, read out Sh, then convert to k<sub>c</sub>.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for kc, and the Reynolds number and boundary layer from fluid mechanics.

blocks.text: At the surface the flux is still diffusive, N<sub>A</sub> = k<sub>c</sub> Δc, but stirring steepens the concentration gradient near the wall and so raises k<sub>c</sub>. Compare this with the purely diffusive flux D<sub>AB</sub> Δc/L over the same length; the ratio is the Sherwood number.

blocks.where: Sh is the Sherwood number (dimensionless), k<sub>c</sub> the mass transfer coefficient in m/s, L the characteristic length in m, D<sub>AB</sub> the diffusivity of A in B in m²/s.

blocks.text: Reynolds number compares inertia with viscous force and decides whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent. Schmidt number compares momentum spreading with mass spreading.
Re = ρ u L / μ = u L / ν      Sc = μ / (ρ D<sub>AB</sub>) = ν / D<sub>AB</sub>
blocks.where: ρ is density in kg/m³, u the free-stream velocity in m/s, μ the viscosity in Pa·s, ν = μ/ρ the kinematic viscosity in m²/s.

blocks.text: Sh does in mass transfer what Nu = hL/k does in heat transfer, and Sc is the mass version of the Prandtl number. Dimensional analysis explains why three groups are enough: k<sub>c</sub> depends on u, L, ρ, μ and D<sub>AB</sub>, six quantities in three dimensions (mass, length, time), so the Buckingham π theorem leaves three groups, and Sh = φ(Re, Sc). Experiment supplies the function φ.
Steady laminar flow over a flat plate of length L, with Re below about 5×10⁵, gives an average coefficient:

blocks.where: averaged over the plate length L, with Re = uL/ν and u the free-stream velocity.

blocks.text: Turbulent from the leading edge on the same plate:

blocks.where: valid roughly from Re = 5×10⁵ to 10⁷; L is the plate length from the leading edge.

blocks.text: A real plate is laminar near the nose and turbulent further on. That mixed plate needs the 871 correction:

blocks.where: the same plate and the same L; the 871 is the laminar stretch subtracted out, not a term to add.

blocks.text: For a single sphere of diameter d in a flowing stream:

blocks.where: L = d. At Re = 0 it returns Sh = 2, pure diffusion to a sphere in still fluid.

blocks.text: The first two are boundary-layer fits for a flat plate; the sphere fit is an empirical correlation for a different geometry, which is why it carries the additive 2. Sc<sup>1/3</sup> appears in all three because the laminar sublayer near the surface controls the mass transfer resistance in each case.

Inside a pipe of diameter d the length is d. In fully developed laminar flow (Re below about 2100) with a constant wall concentration, Sh = 3.66, whatever the velocity; near the entrance Sh is larger. In turbulent flow the wetted-wall column data of Gilliland and Sherwood (vaporisation of liquids into air, Re from about 2000 to 35 000, Sc from 0.6 to 2.5) give:

blocks.where: Sh = k<sub>c</sub> d/D<sub>AB</sub> and Re = ρ u d/μ with d the pipe diameter in m and u the mean velocity in m/s. Linton and Sherwood, using dissolving solid tubes, fitted Sc<sup>1/3</sup> in place of Sc<sup>0.44</sup> for Sc up to about 3000.

blocks.text: Each correlation fixes its own length and its own property temperature. Check both before substituting anything.

items: Pick the geometry: flat plate, single sphere or pipe.
Set L in metres: plate length along the flow, sphere diameter, or pipe diameter.
Evaluate ρ, μ and D<sub>AB</sub> at the film temperature T<sub>f</sub> = (T<sub>s</sub> + T_∞)/2.
Compute ν = μ/ρ, then Re = uL/ν and Sc = ν/D<sub>AB</sub>.
Choose the correlation whose Re range contains your Re; compute Sh.
Convert back: k<sub>c</sub> = Sh D<sub>AB</sub> / L, in m/s.

blocks.text: For gases Sc usually lies between about 0.2 and 3, near 0.6 for water vapour in air; in liquids Sc reaches hundreds or thousands. Outside the tested Re band a correlation is extrapolation, not prediction. Two correlations may share the algebra but not the length: compare definitions, never symbols.

figure.caption: Each correlation drawn only over its fitted range, at the Schmidt numbers of the two worked examples. The flat-plate example (air at 2 m/s over 0.5 m, Re = 6.67×10⁴) sits on the laminar plate line at Sh = 142.7. The wetted-wall pipe at 3.0 m/s gives Sh = 20.7 on the Gilliland–Sherwood line; at 0.30 m/s the flow is laminar and Sh stays at 3.66.

spec.aria: Log-log plot of Sherwood number against Reynolds number from 1e2 to 1e7. A laminar flat-plate line from 1e3 to 5e5 with the point Re 6.67e4, Sh 142.7; a turbulent flat-plate line from 5e5 to 1e7; a flat dashed pipe line at Sh 3.66 up to Re 2100 with a point at Re 469; and a turbulent pipe line from 2000 to 35000 with the point Re 4690, Sh 20.7.

examples.question: Air at 2 m/s flows over a flat plate 0.5 m long, with D<sub>AB</sub> = 2.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s and ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Use Sh = 0.664 Re<sup>1/2</sup> Sc<sup>1/3</sup> to find Re, Sc, Sh and k<sub>c</sub>.
steps: Re = uL/ν = (2 × 0.5)/(1.5×10⁻⁵) = 6.67×10⁴. Below 5×10⁵, so the laminar fit applies.
examples.check:
import math
u = 2.0
L = 0.5
D = 2.6e-5
nu = 1.5e-5
Re = u*L/nu
Sc = nu/D
Sh = 0.664*math.sqrt(Re)*Sc**(1/3)
kc = Sh*D/L
print(round(Re, -2))
print(round(Sc, 3))
print(round(Sh, 1))
print(round(kc, 5))

examples.question: Water evaporates from the inside wall of a wetted-wall column, a pipe of diameter 25 mm. Air at 3.0 m/s flows through it, with ν = 1.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s and D<sub>AB</sub> = 2.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Find k<sub>c</sub>. What would it be at 0.30 m/s?
steps: L = d = 0.025 m. Re = u d/ν = 3.0 × 0.025/1.6×10⁻⁵ = 4690: turbulent, inside the Gilliland–Sherwood range.
At 0.30 m/s, Re = 469: laminar. For a long tube Sh = 3.66, so k<sub>c</sub> = 3.66 × 2.6×10⁻⁵/0.025 = 3.81×10⁻³ m/s.
examples.answer: k<sub>c</sub> ≈ 2.2×10⁻² m/s at 3.0 m/s. A tenth of the velocity gives laminar flow and k<sub>c</sub> ≈ 3.8×10⁻³ m/s, one-sixth as large: in laminar pipe flow k<sub>c</sub> no longer depends on velocity at all.

traps: Using plate length for a sphere or diameter for a plate. Each correlation defines its own L; a wrong L spoils Re and k<sub>c</sub> together.
Evaluating μ and D<sub>AB</sub> at the wall or bulk temperature instead of the film temperature T<sub>f</sub>.

Treating Sh = 0.037 Re<sup>0.8</sup> Sc<sup>1/3</sup> as a whole-plate average. It assumes turbulence from the leading edge; a plate that starts laminar needs Sh = (0.037 Re<sup>0.8</sup> − 871) Sc<sup>1/3</sup>. The correction is a subtraction, not an added laminar term.
Swapping Sh with Nu, or Sc with Pr. The algebra is identical, the symbols are not, and the definition is the first thing marked.

quiz.q: Define Sh and Sc, and give the unit of every symbol in them.
quiz.a: Sh = k<sub>c</sub> L/D<sub>AB</sub>, dimensionless; Sc = μ/(ρD<sub>AB</sub>), dimensionless. k<sub>c</sub> in m/s, L in m, D<sub>AB</sub> in m²/s, μ in Pa·s, ρ in kg/m³.

quiz.q: Why does every correlation here carry the factor Sc<sup>1/3</sup>?
quiz.a: The concentration and velocity boundary layers have thicknesses in the ratio Sc<sup>−1/3</sup>; that factor carries the ratio into Sh.

quiz.q: Why are properties evaluated at the film temperature?
quiz.a: Properties vary across the boundary layer; the mean of wall and bulk, T<sub>f</sub> = (T<sub>s</sub> + T_∞)/2, is the single value the fit was built on.

quiz.q: A 10 mm sphere moves at 0.05 m/s in water with ν = 1.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s and D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁹ m²/s. Find Re, Sc and Sh.
In the worked example, what happens to Sh and k<sub>c</sub> if the velocity doubles?
quiz.a: Re doubles and Sh scales as √2: Sh = 142.7 × 1.414 = 201.8, so k<sub>c</sub> = 201.8 × 2.6×10⁻⁵/0.5 = 1.05×10⁻² m/s.

quiz.q: Two correlations give Sh = 60 and Sh = 900 at the same Re. Give two possible reasons and say how you would choose.
quiz.a: Different geometry or length definition, or a different flow regime (laminar against turbulent). Choose by matching geometry, L definition, Re range and property temperature to your own problem.

beyond: Not for the exam. Rating software stores these fits as tables of j<sub>D</sub> = Sh/(Re Sc<sup>1/3</sup>) against Re, so mass transfer sits beside pressure drop in one database. Research pushes the same idea into microchannels and membrane modules, where Sc runs into the thousands.
